title: Range: the simplest measure of spread
summary: Range = largest value minus smallest value. Easy, but it uses only two numbers.

chunks.heading: What the range is and how to find it
chunks.explanation_md:
The **range** of a data set is the **difference between the largest and the smallest data values**. It is the **simplest measure of variability**.

**Formula:** Range = largest value - smallest value.

**Professor's worked example:** the 70 values are arranged in ascending order, the smallest is 425 and the largest is 615. So **Range = 615 - 425 = 190**.

Tip: sort the data first (the slide notes the data is in ascending order), then subtract the first value from the last.

key_terms.meaning: Largest value minus smallest value; the simplest measure of variability.

chunks.heading: Weaknesses of the range
chunks.explanation_md:
The range is easy but has clear limits, and the professor lists them:

- It is **very sensitive to the smallest and largest values**, so one extreme value changes it a lot.
- It **considers only two values** and ignores the rest of the data set.
- It **does not tell you how the data is distributed between the minimum and maximum**. Two very different data sets can have the same range.

This is why the deck moves on to better measures of spread: the interquartile range, variance and standard deviation.

questions.stem: List three limitations of the range.
questions.model_answer_md:
The range:
1. Is **very sensitive to the smallest and largest values**, so one extreme value changes it a lot.
2. **Considers only two values** and ignores the rest of the data set.
3. **Does not show how the data is distributed** between the minimum and maximum, so two very different data sets can have the same range.

questions.stem: Calculate the sample range for Supplier-1 and Supplier-2 and say what it shows about consistency.
questions.model_answer_md:
Supplier-1 (1 to 11): range = 11 - 1 = **10**.
Supplier-2 (4 to 8): range = 8 - 4 = **4**.

Supplier-2's smaller range means its times are more tightly clustered and so more consistent, even though both have a mean of 6.

questions.stem: Explain the range as a measure of variability: how it is calculated, with the professor's example, its advantages and its limitations.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** The range is the simplest measure of variability. It tells you how wide the data stretches.

**Calculation.** Range = largest value - smallest value. First arrange the data in ascending order, then subtract the first value from the last.

**Professor's example.** For the 70 values, the smallest is 425 and the largest is 615, so **Range = 615 - 425 = 190**.

**Advantages.** It is very easy to compute and to explain.

**Limitations.**
- It is **very sensitive to the smallest and largest data values**.
- It **considers only two values** and ignores all the rest.
- It **does not tell you how the data is distributed** between the minimum and maximum, so two very different data sets can have the same range.

**Link to later measures.** Because the range uses so little information, the deck moves to the interquartile range, variance and standard deviation.

**Conclusion.** Use the range for a quick feel for spread, not for a full comparison.

questions.stem: A company compares two production lines using only the range of daily output. Critically assess this approach, using the idea of the range from the deck, and suggest a better way.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** The range is quick but crude, so judging two lines on it alone can mislead.

**What the range does.** Range = largest value - smallest value. It depends only on two days of output, the best and the worst.

**Problems.**
- It is **very sensitive to the smallest and largest values**: one unusual day changes it a lot.
- It **ignores all the other days**, so it cannot show how the rest of the output is spread.
- **Two very different data sets can have the same range**, so two lines could look equal while one is steady and the other swings.

**Example of the idea in the deck.** The professor's three sets of nine values (Set-1, Set-2 and Set-3) all run from 1 to 9 yet are shaped very differently, so a method using every value is needed.

**Better approach.** Use the **interquartile range** (spread of the middle 50%) to cut the effect of extremes, and the **variance and standard deviation**, which use all the data. To compare lines with different averages, use the **coefficient of variation**.

**Conclusion.** Report the range with a more complete measure of spread before making a decision.
